title: Search Victim-Owned Websites
summary: This technique covers reconnaissance against websites the victim owns, from the home page and staff directory through to support portals and legacy subsites. The target is content that the organisation published deliberately, such as department names, physical sites, named employees with contact details, and partner relationships that hint at who holds trusted access. Beyond reading, the same technique includes discovering what was never linked: crawling sitemap and robots files, and directory enumeration that turns up forgotten pages, old administrative consoles and staging copies. The distinguishing feature relative to searching third party indexes is that the requests hit victim controlled servers, so web access logs, content delivery logs and web application firewall records do capture them. Legitimate crawlers, uptime monitors and penetration testers produce a similar footprint, and defenders separate them by user agent verification, source reputation, request rate and whether the paths requested are ones a normal visitor would ever guess. Abandoned but reachable content is the recurring root cause.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker reads your own website closely. They study your staff pages, contact details, news items and job pages. They may also hunt for old pages and folders that are still reachable but not linked anywhere.
beginner.whyItMatters: Your website tells an attacker who to contact and what the organisation does. Old pages often still work and may have weak security. A slow, careful read of your site can produce a very convincing phishing target list. Unlike reading other sites, these requests reach your servers and can be seen.
howItWorks: The attacker reads your main site to learn your structure, locations and key staff.
They collect names, job titles, email addresses and phone numbers from contact pages.
They check news, press and careers pages for projects, partners and technology choices.
They request files such as sitemap and robots lists that point to areas you prefer to keep quiet.
They try common folder and file names to find forgotten pages or old admin portals.
They record everything and pick the easiest exposed service as a later target.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel where the front desk is tidy but a side corridor still has an old staff door with a worn lock. A visitor reading the public notice board learns the manager's name. A walk down the corridor finds the door. Both are part of the same site, and both help the visitor plan.
takeaways: Treat every reachable page and file as public, even if nothing links to it.
Retire old sites and staging copies instead of leaving them online.
Review web logs for enumeration patterns and verify crawler identities.

objectives: Explain what victim owned website reconnaissance targets and why it works.
Describe how sitemap, robots and directory enumeration expose unlinked content.
Identify the log sources that capture this activity on your own infrastructure.
Distinguish legitimate crawlers and monitoring from hostile enumeration.
Recommend a routine review that retires stale web content.
